title: The court's role in appointing an arbitrator when parties disagree
p1:
What happens when two parties agree to arbitration but cannot agree on the person who will decide the dispute?

Many assume the entire arbitration process stops there. The surprising answer: the court may step in.
p2: A common misconception is that courts replace arbitrators or take over arbitration disputes. In reality, the court's role is usually limited to helping the process move forward when parties fail to make a required appointment.
p3:
If an arbitration agreement exists but the parties cannot agree on an arbitrator, the court can appoint one according to the applicable law. This does not mean the court decides the original dispute. It simply ensures that the agreed dispute-resolution process can begin.

The practical takeaway: a disagreement over choosing an arbitrator does not always end arbitration. The law provides a way to break the deadlock.
conclusion: Did you know a court can help appoint an arbitrator without deciding the actual dispute? Do you think this role protects fairness or gives courts too much involvement?
